title: At the market
goal: Shop for groceries: give quantities, use the partitive article, and handle the conversations that really happen at a produce stall.
bekal: ask for specific amounts using Italian measures

dialogs.title: Dialogo — Dal fruttivendolo
dialogs.intro: An open-air market in the morning. Budi is shopping for the week. In Italy, customers usually don't pick their own fruit — the seller does it for you.

lines.speaker: Venditore:
lines.text: Buongiorno! Mi dica, cosa Le do?
lines.id: Good morning! What can I get you?
lines.literal: good-morning! to-me say, what to-you I-give?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Buongiorno. Vorrei un chilo di pomodori, per favore.
lines.id: Good morning. I'd like a kilo of tomatoes, please.
lines.literal: good-morning. I-would-like a kilo of tomatoes, for favor.

lines.speaker: Venditore:
lines.text: Per l'insalata o per il sugo?
lines.literal: for the salad or for the sauce?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Per il sugo. Perché, sono diversi?
lines.id: For sauce. Why, are they different?
lines.literal: for the sauce. why, are different?

lines.speaker: Venditore:
lines.text: Certo che sono diversi! Prenda questi, sono più maturi.
lines.id: Of course they're different! Take these, they're riper.
lines.literal: certain that are different! take these, are more ripe.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Va bene. Poi mezzo chilo di mele e delle banane.
lines.id: OK. Then half a kilo of apples and some bananas.
lines.literal: goes well. then half kilo of apples and of-the bananas.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Quattro. E un po' di basilico, se c'è.
lines.id: Four. And a little basil, if you have some.
lines.literal: four. and a bit of basil, if there-is.

lines.speaker: Venditore:
lines.text: Il basilico glielo do io. È un regalo.
lines.id: The basil's on me. It's a gift.
lines.literal: the basil to-you-it give I. is a gift.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.id: How kind! How much is it altogether?

lines.speaker: Venditore:
lines.text: Sei euro e ottanta. Facciamo sei e cinquanta.
lines.id: Six euros eighty. Let's say six fifty.
lines.literal: six euro and eighty. we-make six and fifty.

notes: **Cosa Le do?** literally "what do I give you?" — the standard greeting of an Italian seller. You'll hear it at every stall. The informal form is *cosa ti do?*.
**Shop by measure, not by count.** *Un chilo di pomodori*, *mezzo chilo di mele*, *un etto di prosciutto*. Asking for "five tomatoes" might be understood, but it sounds odd.
**Un etto = 100 grams**, the most common measure for cold cuts and cheese: *due etti di prosciutto* = 200 grams. Textbooks rarely teach it, but it's used every day.
**Delle banane = some bananas.** *Di* + a plural article means "some". This is the partitive article, and Italian uses it where English often says "some" or nothing at all.
**Un po' di also means a little, but for things you can't count.** *Un po' di pane*, *un po' di acqua*, *un po' di basilico*. If you can count it, use *qualche* or *alcuni*.

**Don't touch the fruit yourself.** At traditional Italian markets and many greengrocers, picking produce with your own hands is considered rude. Just say what you want; the seller picks it, and usually picks better than you would.
**Facciamo sei e cinquanta** — the seller rounds down. This isn't haggling; market prices in Italy are fixed. The small rounding and the free basil are friendliness, not negotiation.
**Glielo do io** packs two little words together — *gli* + *lo*. This form is beyond A1; for now just recognize it. What matters: the seller is saying the basil is free.

grammars.title: The partitive article — some, a little
body: It's made from *di* + the article, and it means "an unspecified amount".
after: ⚠️ *Qualche* is always followed by a **singular** noun even though the meaning is plural: *qualche amico*, not *qualche amici*. Just memorize this exception as it is.
In negative sentences the partitive is dropped: *Non ho pane* (I don't have any bread), not *non ho del pane*.

grammars.title: Measures and containers
body: All of them link to the noun with *di*, and here *di* does **not** merge with an article.
after: Note *un chilo di pane*, not *un chilo del pane*. After a measure, the noun stands bare with no article.

blocks.text: *L'uovo* is the oddest word on this list: masculine in the singular, but feminine in the plural with an -a ending — *le uova*. A small group of nouns behaves this way, and eggs are the one you'll use most.

blocks.title: Ready-made phrases for the shop
items: *Vorrei un chilo di…* — I'd like a kilo of…
*Quanto costa al chilo?* — How much per kilo?
*Avete del pane fresco?* — Do you have fresh bread?
*Posso avere un sacchetto?* — Can I have a bag?

blocks.text: *Basta così* is the most common way to wrap up your shopping, and it's handy at restaurants too when you don't want anything more.
